idiom_name: System.Reflection.DispatchProxy<T, TProxy> with an Invoke override
implementation_notes: The in-box mechanism is System.Reflection.DispatchProxy: derive a proxy class from DispatchProxy<T, TProxy>, and Create<T, TProxy>() returns an instance that implements the interface T and routes every interface call to your Invoke(MethodInfo, object[]) override, which is where the membrane wraps arguments, forwards to the wrapped target and wraps the result - the forwarding half of the classic structure is generated by the runtime. DispatchProxy proxies interfaces only, so a membrane over a class must either expose an interface or move to a bytecode library (Castle DynamicProxy or a source-generated interceptor). Identity and revocation stay the membrane's own: keep a ConditionalWeakTable or an identity-keyed map so one target yields one wrapper, and a single revocation flag checked before forwarding; the reflection dispatch of Invoke is the price of getting total mediation without writing a forwarding member per method.
pitfalls: DispatchProxy supports interfaces only; class targets need a bytecode proxy, which is a design constraint on the mediated surface rather than a detail.

Invoke is a reflection call per method with arguments boxed in object[]: arrays, ref/out parameters and generic methods have to be wrapped explicitly, and a wrong wrapper type surfaces as a TargetException rather than a compile error.
The generated proxy has its own reference identity; without an identity map callers comparing targets see two wrappers for one object, and without weak keys the map pins the wrapped graph.
